stem.en: A classmate has two clear liquids: 10 g of salt in 100 mL of solution, and 0.9 g of salt in 100 mL of solution. "Both pass all three tests, so they are the same," she says. What is the best reply?

text.en: "Both are solutions, but the tests do not measure how much salt is in each one."
"You are right. A solution is a solution, so either one can be used for anything."
"Only the 10 g one is a solution. The other has too little salt to count as a solution."
"You must have done the tests badly. Done with care, they would show a difference."

explanation.en: The tests are right: both liquids are solutions. But the tests only show that a mixture is uniform. They do not measure how much is dissolved, so "both are solutions" does not mean "the same". Option b makes that mistake. Option c fails because a solution can be very dilute. Option d fails because repeating the tests would give the same results.

hints.en: List the three tests. Does any of them measure an amount?
Being a solution and how much is dissolved are two different questions.
